methods.title: About
methods.about: hilal.day is a free, open-source tool for exploring the Islamic (Hijri) calendar. It lets you browse monthly calendars, convert dates between Hijri and Gregorian, view upcoming Islamic holidays, and inspect astronomical crescent-visibility estimates for any location. All calculations run entirely in your browser — no data is sent to any server.

keyConcepts.title: Key Astronomical Concepts
keyConcepts.intro: All crescent-visibility models rely on four measurable quantities computed at the moment of local sunset. Understanding these helps interpret the scores shown throughout the app.
keyConcepts.altitude: The angle of the moon above the observer's horizon at the moment of sunset, measured in degrees. If h ≤ 0°, the moon is below the horizon and cannot be seen. A higher altitude gives the crescent more contrast against the twilight sky. Typical range for a young crescent: −5° to +15°.
keyConcepts.elongation: The angular separation between the moon and the sun as seen from Earth, measured in degrees. Below about 6° (the Danjon limit), the crescent has never been reliably observed with any instrument. Greater elongation means a wider, brighter crescent.
keyConcepts.moonAge: The time elapsed since the last sun–moon conjunction (astronomical new moon), measured in hours. A crescent younger than about 12 hours is essentially invisible. Between 15–24 hours it may become visible under ideal conditions. Beyond 72 hours it is no longer a ‘new’ crescent.
keyConcepts.lag: The time difference between sunset and moonset, measured in minutes. If L ≤ 0, the moon sets before the sun and the crescent is not observable. A larger lag gives more time to spot the crescent in the darkening sky after sunset.
keyConcepts.glossaryTitle: Other Terms Used in This App
keyConcepts.conjunction: The moment when the sun and moon have the same ecliptic longitude as seen from Earth. This is the astronomical new moon — the moon is between the Earth and the sun, and its illuminated side faces away from us. It marks the starting point from which moon age (A) is measured. The crescent becomes potentially visible only some hours after conjunction.
keyConcepts.danjon: An observational lower bound on the moon–sun elongation below which the lunar crescent has never been reliably observed. André Danjon (1936) estimated it at about 7°; Odeh (2004) refined it to 6.4°. All visibility models in this app treat elongation below this limit as ‘not visible’.
keyConcepts.arcv: The angular difference in altitude between the moon and the sun at sunset, measured in degrees. Used by the Yallop and Odeh methods as a primary predictor. A larger ARCV means the moon is higher above the sun at the horizon — making the crescent easier to see.
keyConcepts.crescentWidth: The apparent angular width of the illuminated crescent as seen from the observer’s location, measured in arc-minutes. Wider crescents are brighter and easier to spot. Yallop and Odeh both use W’ in their polynomial formulas.
keyConcepts.illumination: The fraction of the moon’s visible disc that is lit by the sun, expressed as a percentage. At conjunction it is ~0%; at full moon it is 100%. For a young crescent (the first 1–3 days), illumination typically ranges from 0% to about 10%. This value is shown in the calendar and detail views.
keyConcepts.waxingWaning: After conjunction the illuminated portion grows each day — this is waxing (crescent → first quarter → full). After full moon it shrinks — this is waning. Only the waxing crescent in the first 72 hours after conjunction is relevant for ‘new month’ detection; a waning moon automatically receives a score of 0.

civil.ch2: Months alternate 30/29 days; month 12 is 30 in leap years

civil.pro1: Stable and predictable; no external data needed
civil.pro2: Works offline and is easy to test
civil.con1: May differ from official country calendars
civil.con2: Does not reflect actual crescent visibility

estimate.title: Hilal.day heuristic
estimate.summary: A simplified educational index created by Hilal.day. It combines the young crescent's altitude, elongation, age, and moonset lag for a given evening and location. It is not a published visibility criterion and not a probability of human observation.
estimate.step1title: Step 1 — Compute astronomical values at local sunset
estimate.step1: Using the astronomy-engine library, the app computes for the selected location at the moment of sunset: moon altitude (h), moon–sun elongation (Δ), moon age since last conjunction (A), and moonset lag after sunset (L).
estimate.step2title: Step 2 — Normalize each value to a 0–1 scale
estimate.step2: Each raw value is mapped linearly into the range [0, 1] using a low and high threshold. The formula is: score = (value − low) / (high − low), then if the result is below 0 it becomes 0, and if above 1 it becomes 1.
estimate.step2hDesc: Moon altitude at sunset. 0° = horizon (moon not visible below it). 10° = well above atmospheric haze and extinction — crescent is comfortably visible.
estimate.step2elongDesc: Moon–sun elongation. 6° = Danjon limit — the minimum separation at which a crescent has ever been reliably observed. 15° = elongation at which naked-eye sighting becomes comfortable.
estimate.step2ageDesc: Moon age since conjunction. 12 h = youngest crescent ever claimed sighted (record observations). 24 h = by this age the crescent is typically well-formed enough for easy sighting.
estimate.step2lagDesc: Moonset lag after sunset. 0 min = moon sets with the sun, so there is no observation window. 60 min = ample time for the sky to darken and the crescent to stand out.
estimate.ex2label: Low (11–35%) — crescent may be glimpsed under ideal conditions
estimate.step3: The weights reflect that altitude and elongation are the strongest predictors of naked-eye crescent visibility.
estimate.step4a: If the moon age > 72 h or the moon is in its waning half (past full moon): score = 0 (not a new-month crescent).
estimate.step4b: If altitude ≤ 0° or elongation < 6° (Danjon limit) or age < 12 h: score is capped at 0.20 (crescent is almost certainly not visible).
estimate.step4c: If altitude ≥ 7° AND elongation ≥ 12° AND age ≥ 20 h: score is at least 0.75 (crescent is almost certainly visible).
estimate.step5: Visibility % = round(score × 100). The label is assigned as: None (0%), Faint (1–10%), Low (11–35%), Fair (36–65%), High (> 65%).
estimate.exclusivity: If day X receives a Fair or High signal, day X+1 is forced to None (0%). This prevents two consecutive days from both being labeled as potential month starts.
estimate.input1: h = Moon altitude above horizon at sunset (degrees). Range: typically −5° to +15° for a young crescent.
estimate.input2: Δ = Geocentric elongation between moon and sun (degrees). Below ~6° the crescent has never been reliably observed (Danjon limit).
estimate.input3: A = Moon age = hours elapsed since the last sun–moon conjunction (new moon). A crescent younger than ~12 h is essentially invisible.
estimate.input4: L = Moonset lag = minutes between sunset and moonset. If L ≤ 0, the moon has already set when the sun sets.
estimate.note: Important: this is an astronomical estimate, not an official religious announcement. The actual start of Islamic months is determined by religious authorities in each country.
estimate.impl: Astronomical engine: astronomy-engine (npm) — computes sun/moon ephemeris for any date and location.

yallop.title: Yallop q-test (1997)
yallop.summary: A single-parameter lunar crescent visibility test developed by B. D. Yallop of HM Nautical Almanac Office. It computes a q-value from the arc of vision (ARCV) and topocentric crescent width (W'), classifying visibility into six zones (A–F).
yallop.ch1: Computes best observation time Tb = Ts + (4/9) × Lag, where Ts = sunset, Lag = moonset − sunset.
yallop.ch3: Classifies the crescent into zones A–F based on q-value thresholds.
yallop.zoneA: Zone A (q > 0.216): easily visible with naked eye.
yallop.zoneB: Zone B (−0.014 < q ≤ 0.216): visible under perfect conditions.
yallop.zoneC: Zone C (−0.160 < q ≤ −0.014): may need optical aid to find crescent.
yallop.zoneD: Zone D (−0.232 < q ≤ −0.160): will need optical aid to find crescent.
yallop.zoneE: Zone E (−0.293 < q ≤ −0.232): not visible even with a telescope.
yallop.zoneF: Zone F (q ≤ −0.293): below Danjon limit — not visible.
yallop.note: Optical-aid sighting (zones C–D) is accepted by many Islamic jurisprudential schools, so those zones are mapped to Fair. Zones A–B (naked-eye) map to High, while E–F map to Faint/None.

odeh.title: Odeh criterion (2004)
odeh.summary: A refined single-parameter crescent visibility criterion developed by Mohammad Sh. Odeh, calibrated against 737 observations. It computes a V-value from the arc of vision (ARCV) and topocentric crescent width (W'), classifying visibility into four zones (A–D).
odeh.ch1: Computes best observation time Tb = Ts + (4/9) × Lag (same as Yallop).
odeh.ch2: Uses a cubic polynomial: V = ARCV − (−0.1018·W'³ + 0.7319·W'² − 6.3226·W' + 7.1651). Note: V is NOT divided by 10.
odeh.ch3: Classifies the crescent into 4 zones (A–D) based on V-value thresholds, with a Danjon limit of 6.4°.
odeh.zoneA: Zone A (V ≥ 5.65): crescent visible by naked eye.
odeh.zoneB: Zone B (2 ≤ V < 5.65): visible by optical aid; may be seen by naked eye.
odeh.zoneC: Zone C (−0.96 ≤ V < 2): crescent visible by optical aid only.
odeh.zoneD: Zone D (V < −0.96): not visible, even with optical aid.
odeh.note: Optical-aid sighting (zone C) is accepted by many Islamic jurisprudential schools, so it is mapped to Fair. Zones A–B (naked-eye possible) map to High, while D maps to Low/None.

schaefer.title: Schaefer criterion (1988 / 1996)
schaefer.summary: A physically-motivated model developed by Bradley E. Schaefer that accounts for atmospheric extinction, sky brightness, and the physiological threshold of the human eye. Rather than a single polynomial, Schaefer builds a forward model of contrast between the lunar crescent and the twilight sky, then compares it against empirical visibility thresholds.

sultan.title: SAAO / Sultan criterion (2006)
sultan.summary: An empirical criterion developed by Abdul Haq Sultan at the South African Astronomical Observatory using a dataset of 2,401 observations. It defines a visibility curve in the (DAZ, ARCV) plane, where DAZ is the relative azimuth difference between the sun and moon at sunset.

danjon.title: Danjon limit
danjon.summary: An observational lower bound on the geocentric elongation below which the lunar crescent has never been reliably observed. André Danjon (1936) estimated this limit at about 7°; later Odeh (2004) refined it to 6.4° and Schaefer (1991) suggested it may vary with atmospheric conditions. Methods like Yallop and Odeh incorporate a Danjon cut-off; if elongation is below this limit, the crescent is automatically classified as not visible.

babylonian.title: Babylonian / Lag-based rule
babylonian.summary: One of the oldest known empirical rules, dating back to Babylonian astronomy: the crescent is declared visible when the moonset lag (time between sunset and moonset) exceeds a fixed threshold, typically about 48 minutes. This simple rule captures the basic idea that the moon must be above the horizon long enough after sunset, but it ignores factors such as elongation, atmospheric extinction, and location.

mabims.title: MABIMS 2016 / Imkanur Rukyat
mabims.summary: A published, multi-country crescent visibility criterion adopted in 2016 by MABIMS — the joint religious authority of Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, and Singapore. It tightens the older MABIMS thresholds to better match observed crescent sightings.
mabims.pro1: Published, regionally adopted criterion — defensible reference
mabims.pro2: All thresholds are simple geometric numbers; results are reproducible
mabims.con1: Stricter than the in-house heuristic — predicts fewer month-starts
mabims.con2: Calibrated for South-East Asia; may be conservative for Middle East / North Africa
mabims.note: Adopted in 2016 by Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, and Singapore as a joint criterion (replacing the older MABIMS thresholds of altitude ≥ 2°, elongation ≥ 3°, age ≥ 8h). Historical accuracy on 164 official declarations across 5 countries (AH 1427–1447): 52% exact match, mean absolute difference 1.71 days.

probability.label: Month-start signal
probability.noChanceHint: This evening cannot mark a new Hijri month start (we're not near a new moon, or the Moon sets at/before sunset).
probability.disclaimer: The month-start signal is an astronomical classification for the evening (around local sunset) at the selected location. It is not an official religious announcement.
probability.eveningEstimateHint: Estimate for this evening; it affects the next day after sunset.
probability.skyPositionHint: The horizon view shows where the Moon sits relative to the local western horizon and the Sun at sunset.
probability.whyHeuristic: The Hilal.day heuristic combines altitude, elongation, lunar age, and moonset lag into an educational month-start index.
probability.whyYallop: Yallop uses q and zone thresholds from a published crescent-visibility criterion, evaluated near the best observation time after sunset.
probability.whyOdeh: Odeh uses V and zone thresholds from a published crescent-visibility criterion, evaluated near the best observation time after sunset.
probability.whyCaveat: This is an astronomical classification for the selected location and method, not an official religious declaration.
probability.noChanceDesc: The crescent test was run for tonight and conditions rule out a month-start signal (for example, the Moon sets at or before sunset, or the index is too low).
probability.veryLowDesc: Extremely weak conditions; crescent is unlikely visible and confidence for month start is minimal.
probability.lowDesc: Poor conditions for a visible crescent (e.g., Moon very low, setting too soon, or very young).
probability.mediumDesc: Borderline/mixed conditions; visibility depends on observer skill and local atmosphere.
probability.highDesc: Strong conditions (Moon higher, well separated from the Sun, older, stays up longer after sunset).
probability.mostLikelyDesc: When several days score positively, the highest-scoring candidate is highlighted with a star.
probability.notApplicableDesc: We are not near a new moon — the crescent test does not apply right now. The Moon is visible, but no Hijri month can start tonight.
probability.notApplicableHint: Mid-Hijri-month: this evening is not a candidate for a new month. The crescent test only applies in the last days of the current Hijri month.

scholars.title: Scholarly Views on the Hijri Calendar
scholars.subtitle: Why Islamic scholars differ on when a new lunar month begins
scholars.intro: The Islamic (Hijri) calendar is a purely lunar calendar. Each month begins with the sighting of the new crescent moon (hilal). However, Islamic scholars have held different views for centuries on exactly how to determine that beginning — leading to situations where Ramadan, Eid, and other occasions may start on different days in different countries, or even within the same country — especially in geographically large nations where the crescent may be visible in one region but not another. Historically, though, each country has had a single religious authority (such as a mufti, sighting committee, or ministry of religious affairs) that issues a binding declaration for the entire country.
scholars.coreQuestion: The Core Question: How Is the New Moon Determined?
scholars.coreQuestionBody: All scholars agree that the Islamic month begins with the crescent moon — but they differ on several key points: Must the crescent be physically sighted with the naked eye, or can astronomical calculations suffice? If sighted, must it be seen locally, or does a confirmed sighting anywhere in the world count? Should optical instruments (telescopes, binoculars) be used? These questions have produced distinct scholarly positions, each rooted in Quranic verses, Hadith, and centuries of jurisprudential reasoning (ijtihad).

localSighting.title: Position 1: Local Sighting (Ikhtilaf al-Matali')
localSighting.body: This position holds that each region or country should rely on its own local crescent sighting. A sighting in Saudi Arabia, for example, does not obligate Muslims in Indonesia or Morocco to begin the month. The reasoning is that the moon's visibility varies by geographic location — the crescent may be visible in one part of the world but not yet in another.
localSighting.scholars: Imam al-Shafi'i, and the majority of the Shafi'i school. Also supported by many Hanbali scholars. Adopted by several Southeast Asian countries and by Egypt's Dar al-Ifta.
localSighting.practice: Countries like Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, and Egypt each conduct their own sighting and may start Ramadan on a different day than other countries. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta relies on local sighting confirmed by its own crescent observation committees across the country, and often announces dates that differ from Saudi Arabia by a day.

globalSighting.title: Position 2: Global Sighting (Ittihad al-Matali')
globalSighting.body: This position holds that if the crescent is reliably sighted anywhere in the world, all Muslims should begin the new month. The argument is based on the generality of the Prophet's hadith: 'Fast when you see it [the crescent] and break fast when you see it' — interpreting 'you' as the entire Muslim Ummah, not just a local community.
globalSighting.scholars: Predominant view among Hanafi scholars. Supported by some Hanbali scholars. Also adopted by the Fiqh Council of the Muslim World League in some rulings.
globalSighting.practice: Some Muslim communities in the West follow the earliest confirmed sighting globally (often from Saudi Arabia or the Middle East) to start their fast.

calculation.title: Position 3: Astronomical Calculation
calculation.body: A growing number of scholars and institutions argue that modern astronomical science can reliably predict when the crescent will be visible. They hold that calculations are at least as trustworthy as fallible human eyesight, and that the hadith about sighting was addressing a community without astronomical knowledge — not prohibiting the use of science. Some proponents distinguish between 'born moon' (conjunction) and 'visible crescent' calculations.
calculation.scholars: Supported by Yusuf al-Qaradawi, the Fiqh Council of North America (FCNA), the European Council for Fatwa and Research (ECFR), and many contemporary scholars. The FCNA officially adopted astronomical calculation in 2006.
calculation.practice: Turkey has used a purely calculated calendar (based on the Diyanet) for decades. The FCNA and ISNA in North America publish Ramadan and Eid dates years in advance based on calculations.

followSaudi.title: Position 4: Follow Saudi Arabia
followSaudi.body: Some communities choose to follow Saudi Arabia's announcement regardless of their own local sighting, arguing for unity with the land of the Two Holy Mosques (Haramain). This is not strictly a scholarly position on moon-sighting methodology, but rather a practical choice made by certain communities and organizations.
followSaudi.practice: Common among some diaspora communities who prefer a single reference point. Several countries in the Middle East and South Asia have historically aligned with Saudi announcements.

instruments.title: Naked Eye vs. Optical Instruments
instruments.body: Another point of debate is whether the crescent must be seen with the unaided naked eye or can be confirmed using telescopes, binoculars, or CCD imaging. Classical scholars naturally assumed naked-eye observation. Today, most sighting committees accept optical aids, but some traditionalist scholars insist only a naked-eye sighting fulfills the hadith. This can cause a one-day difference: a crescent too thin for the naked eye may be visible through a telescope.

whyDiffer.title: Why Do Countries Announce Different Dates?
whyDiffer.body: Even when two countries use the same general approach (e.g., both rely on sighting), they may still differ for several reasons:
whyDiffer.reason1: Geographic location — the crescent is visible in western longitudes before eastern ones on the same night.
whyDiffer.reason2: Weather and atmospheric conditions — clouds, dust, or haze can prevent sighting even when the moon is astronomically above the horizon.
whyDiffer.reason3: Criteria stringency — some committees accept a single witness testimony; others require multiple witnesses or corroborating evidence.
whyDiffer.reason4: Political considerations — some governments align with regional allies or make announcements based on diplomatic factors.
whyDiffer.reason5: Methodology mix — some countries use calculations to reject impossible sightings but still require a physical sighting for confirmation (a hybrid approach).

scholars.disclaimer: This page is for educational purposes only. It presents a simplified overview of scholarly positions and does not constitute a religious ruling (fatwa). Muslims are advised to follow their local Islamic authority or trusted scholarly body for determining the start of Islamic months.

about.title: About
about.privacyBody: Your privacy matters. Calendar features and calculations run in your browser:
about.privacyNoServer: All date and astronomical calculations happen locally on your device; calculation inputs are not sent to a server.
about.privacyNoTracking: We use GoatCounter to collect privacy-friendly aggregate page-view statistics. It does not use tracking cookies or persistent identifiers.
about.privacyNoCookies: Neither this app nor GoatCounter stores visitor cookies. Your preferences (language, location, method) stay in your browser's local storage and are not shared with GoatCounter.
about.privacyLocation: If you choose to share your location, it is used only for local sunset/moonset calculations and is never transmitted anywhere.
about.disclaimerBody: This tool is for informational and educational purposes only. It is not an official religious authority and should not be used as a substitute for local moon-sighting committees or official Hijri calendar announcements in your country. Crescent-visibility estimates are based on astronomical models and may differ from actual observed conditions.
about.featureCalendar: Monthly Hijri calendar view showing all 12 Islamic months — Muharram, Safar, Rabi' al-Awwal, Rabi' al-Thani, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Thani, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul Qi'dah, and Dhul Hijjah — alongside the Gregorian months (January through December).
about.featureHolidays: Estimated dates for key Islamic holidays: Ramadan start, Eid al-Fitr (1 Shawwal), Eid al-Adha (10 Dhul Hijjah), Islamic New Year (1 Muharram), Day of Arafah, and Ashura (10 Muharram).
about.featureConvert: Instant Gregorian-to-Hijri and Hijri-to-Gregorian date converter supporting multiple calculation methods.
about.featureMethods: Crescent moon (hilal) visibility estimation using the Yallop q-test criterion, Odeh visibility criterion, geometric sunset model, and the tabular Islamic civil calendar. Includes moon altitude, elongation, age, moonset lag, and illumination data.
about.featureHistory: Historical comparison of officially declared Hijri month starts (Saudi Arabia and other countries) against astronomically calculated predictions.
about.featureMonths: Scientific reference covering 15+ methods: Yallop, Odeh, Schaefer, SAAO, Danjon limit, Babylonian lag rule, Fotheringham, Maunder, Indian, Malaysian, and the Umm al-Qura calendar.
about.featureBilingual: Fully bilingual interface in English and Arabic with right-to-left (RTL) support.
about.openSourceBody: hilal.day is free and open-source software. Contributions, bug reports, and suggestions are welcome.
about.ourResearchDesc: Our comprehensive survey of 15 Hijri month-start methods, with formulae, pseudocode, and citations from the academic literature

today.short: See today's Hijri date and today's Gregorian date side by side, with tonight's crescent moon visibility and a countdown to the next Islamic holiday.
today.more: The Today page converts the current Gregorian date to the Hijri (Islamic) date using your chosen calculation method and location. It also shows the moon's altitude, elongation, age, and illumination at sunset, so you can judge whether a new Hijri month is likely to begin tonight.

calendar.short: Browse a monthly Hijri calendar aligned with the Gregorian months, and see which days are likely to start a new Islamic month.
calendar.more: Each cell pairs the Gregorian day with its Hijri date. Around month boundaries the calendar highlights candidate days for the new crescent, so you can see where Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, or Eid al-Adha may fall for your location and method.

convert.short: Convert any Gregorian date to Hijri, or any Hijri date to Gregorian — including birth dates and historical dates.
convert.more: Enter a Gregorian day, month, and year to get the matching Hijri date, or enter a Hijri date to get the Gregorian one. Results follow the calculation method you select, and you can copy the result in several formats.

holidays.short: Find the estimated dates of Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Ashura, the Day of Arafah, and the Islamic New Year.
holidays.more: Islamic holidays depend on when each Hijri month begins, so these dates are estimates rather than official announcements. Expand a holiday to see the candidate dates and how likely the crescent is to be sighted on each.

details.short: Inspect the day-by-day astronomical data behind each Hijri month start: moon altitude, elongation, age, moonset lag, and illumination.
details.more: This page shows the numbers the visibility criteria actually use. It is aimed at readers who want to check the reasoning behind a predicted month start rather than only the final date.

visibilityMap.short: See where in the world the moon is above the horizon at sunset, and — near a month boundary — where the new crescent could be sighted.
visibilityMap.more: The top map always shows the moon's altitude at local sunset. For roughly half of every lunar month the moon is below the horizon at sunset because it is waning and rises later at night; this is normal, not an error. The second map appears only around a Hijri month boundary, when a new crescent could realistically be sighted.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.intro: Short answers to the questions we get asked most about the Hijri calendar.
faq.qb1: How do I convert a Gregorian date to a Hijri date?
faq.ab1: Open the Convert page, enter the Gregorian day, month, and year, and the matching Hijri date appears instantly. You can also convert in the other direction, from Hijri to Gregorian, which is useful for birth dates and historical dates.
faq.qb2: How do I find today's Hijri date?
faq.ab2: The Today page shows the current Hijri and Gregorian date for your selected location, along with tonight's crescent visibility and the next Islamic holiday.
faq.qb3: Why do Hijri dates differ between countries?
faq.ab3: The Hijri month begins when the new crescent is sighted, and visibility depends on your location, the weather, and the criterion each authority applies. This is why neighbouring countries can start a month on different days.
faq.qb4: Why do Hijri months have 29 or 30 days?
faq.ab4: A lunar month lasts about 29.53 days, so it cannot be a whole number of days. Each Hijri month therefore runs 29 or 30 days depending on whether the crescent is seen on the 29th evening.
faq.qh1: When are Ramadan and Eid this year?
faq.ah1: The Holidays page lists estimated dates for Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Ashura, the Day of Arafah, and the Islamic New Year, with a countdown to the next ones. These are estimates: your country's official announcement may differ by a day.
faq.qh2: Can I add Islamic holidays to my calendar?
faq.ah2: Yes. On the Holidays page each row has an add-to-calendar button, and one button adds every listed holiday at once. The downloaded .ics file works with Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, and Outlook.
faq.qh3: How many days are left until Ramadan?
faq.ah3: The countdown at the top of the Holidays page, and the dedicated Countdown page, both show the days remaining until each upcoming Islamic date for your chosen method and location.
faq.qm1: Which calculation method should I choose?
faq.am1: If you are unsure, keep the default and compare the alternatives on the Methods page. If you follow a particular country's announcements, the History page shows which method has matched that country most often.
faq.qm2: What are Tabular, MABIMS, Yallop, and Odeh?
faq.am2: Tabular is a fixed arithmetic calendar that needs no observation. MABIMS applies fixed thresholds for moon altitude, elongation, age, and moonset lag. Yallop and Odeh are published criteria that score the crescent against observation records and report a visibility zone.
faq.qm3: Which method is the most accurate?
faq.am3: There is no single winner: accuracy depends on the country and the years compared. The History page scores every method against real official declarations across 15 countries and 21 Hijri years so you can judge for yourself.
faq.qm4: Is calculation allowed, or must the crescent be sighted?
faq.am4: Scholars differ. Some require local sighting, some accept a sighting anywhere, some accept calculation, and some follow one central authority. The Scholars page explains each position without endorsing one; this site calculates, it does not issue rulings.
faq.qu1: Why does the visibility map show the moon below the horizon for days at a time?
faq.au1: That is expected. After the full moon the moon is waning, so at sunset it has not yet risen and its altitude is negative. This lasts for roughly half of every lunar month and reverses a day or two after the new moon, when the waxing crescent appears above the horizon again.
faq.qu2: The date here is one day off from my mosque. Why?
faq.au2: A one-day difference is normal: authorities apply different criteria, and some wait for a confirmed local sighting. Switch to the calculation method your country follows — the History page shows which method has matched each country's official announcements most often.
faq.qu3: Does this site track me or need an internet connection?
faq.au3: Every calculation runs in your browser, and your location never leaves your device. Only anonymous, cookie-free page counts are recorded. Once loaded, the site is installable and keeps working offline.
faq.qu4: What makes this Hijri calendar different?
faq.au4: It compares several published methods side by side instead of committing to one, shows the astronomical numbers behind every prediction, and reports how each method scored against real official declarations. It is free, open source, and works offline.
